attempts.answer:
Yes. A large and diverse ecosystem of reasoning benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) has emerged across math/logic, science/commonsense, code/tool use, and multimodal/creative problem solving, with many designed to stress long chains of inference, domain knowledge, and robustness beyond simple memorization. <cite id="b453ef15-0">Numerous reasoning benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate various cognitive skills, including visual mathematical reasoning, spatial understanding, analogical reasoning, and social reasoning, alongside broad academic and real-world reasoning suites such as HEMM, SciBench, MMMU/MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-1">General and reasoning-focused benchmarks such as MMLU, MMLU‑Pro, GLUE, SuperGLUE, CommonSenseQA, BIG‑Bench, ARC‑Challenge, BoolQ, HellaSwag, SQuAD, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, and MATH have substantially expanded evaluation coverage, but near‑perfect results by frontier models have motivated more challenging testbeds</cite>.

Below is a practical overview by category, with representative benchmarks, what they measure, and typical evaluation protocols.

Taxonomy of reasoning benchmarks and exemplars

Math and logic reasoning
- Core math word-problem and multi-step derivations: GSM8K (grade-school math word problems with short numeric answers), MATH500 (a 500-problem subset of competition-level math requiring longer, multistep derivations), and AIME 2024/2025 (competition-style integer answers). <cite id="382b0788-0">GSM8K consists of grade-school math word problems with short numerical answers; MATH500 is a 500-problem evaluation subset of competition-level math requiring longer, multistep derivations; AIME 2024/2025 require producing a final integer answer and further stress long-horizon reasoning</cite> <cite id="382b0788-3">For GSM8K and MATH500, chain-of-thought prompting is commonly used and evaluated by Exact Match accuracy via a rule-based numerical answer parser; MATH500 reflects competition-level logical consistency demands</cite>. 
- Harder academic math: MATH500 and newer AIME-style sets push beyond GSM8K; meta-reasoning and decoding papers also list MATH500 and AIME among top long-horizon reasoning testbeds. <cite id="382b0788-1">MATH500 and AIME24/AIME25 appear across many reasoning-method papers alongside GSM8K</cite> <cite id="382b0788-4">Evaluation on MATH500 and AIME2024 uses model-specific templates with boxed expression parsing for answers</cite>.

Science, commonsense, and multihop reasoning
- Multisubject university-level knowledge and reasoning: MMLU (57 tasks across STEM/humanities/social sciences) and its enhanced, harder variant MMLU‑Pro (12,032 questions across 14 subjects with 10 choices per question to reduce guessing). <cite id="b453ef15-1">MMLU and MMLU‑Pro are central general/knowledge benchmarks used to assess complex reasoning</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-0">MMLU‑Pro expands to 10 answer options per question, filters out trivial items, and increases difficulty to improve discriminative power</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-1">MMLU‑Pro improves robustness via 10-way choices and model-based/expert filtering of low-difficulty items</cite>. 
- Graduate-level, web-“proof” resistant science: GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof QA), especially the GPQA‑Diamond 198-question subset authored by domain experts with human expert accuracy near 65% and designed to be hard even for non-experts. <cite id="52760b4f-0">GPQA Diamond comprises 198 graduate-level questions across biology, chemistry, and physics; human expert accuracy is around 65% and questions are designed to be difficult even outside one’s specialty</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-1">GPQA is a high-difficulty multiple-choice benchmark authored by domain experts, with the Diamond subset selected for quality and difficulty; evaluation uses accuracy and abstention</cite>. 
- Additional graduate/theorem-level science: TheoremQA (800 theorem-application problems) and ARC‑Challenge (700 commonsense reasoning items). <cite id="52760b4f-2">Graduate-level evaluations include GPQA Diamond (198), TheoremQA (800), MMLU‑Pro (490 multisubject reasoning problems with 10 options), and ARC‑Challenge (700 commonsense questions)</cite>.

Code and tool-use reasoning
- Code generation and unit-test correctness: HumanEval (functional correctness on small programs) and MBPP (more diverse, few-shot tasks), commonly reported with Pass@1. <cite id="382b0788-3">For HumanEval and MBPP, functional correctness is evaluated with Pass@1; HumanEval tests zero-shot handwritten problems while MBPP uses a few-shot setup</cite> <cite id="382b0788-2">HumanEval and MBPP are standard code-generation benchmarks alongside MetaEval-style suites</cite>. 
- Broader tool-use/code reasoning suites: LiveCodeBench and related corpora are increasingly used to test practical coding and tool integration. <cite id="382b0788-2">Code generation benchmarks include MBPP, HumanEval, and Live-CodeBench</cite>. 
- Hard math-to-code bridges: Some math/math-competition benchmarks (MATH500, AIME) are often paired with code-generation evaluations to stress end-to-end problem solving. <cite id="382b0788-3">MATH500 is used to probe high-precision reasoning and long derivations</cite> <cite id="382b0788-0">AIME 2024/2025 provide competition-style numeric outputs under high difficulty</cite>.

Multimodal, creative, and olympiad-style reasoning
- Cross-disciplinary academic and real-world reasoning: HEMM, SciBench, MMMU/MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench target multimodal and abstract, open-ended problems. <cite id="b453ef15-0">HEMM, SciBench, MMMU/MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench are designed to test multimodal reasoning and abstract, open-ended problems across disciplines</cite>. 
- Linguistics/anthropology-style pattern puzzles: International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL) tasks probe pattern recognition and domain adaptation; recent work studies why LLMs lag and whether inference-time scaling helps. <cite id="b453ef15-2">LLMs perform strongly on arithmetic and coding benchmarks but significantly worse on International Linguistics Olympiad tasks; recent work explores whether inference-time scaling can close the gap</cite>. 
- New “olympiad” math/CS suites: Olympiad‑Bench aggregates competition-style problems; AIME/GPQA Diamond extend to advanced reasoning. <cite id="b453ef15-0">Olympiad‑Bench targets academic and real-world reasoning with abstract problems</cite> <cite id="382b0788-0">AIME 2024/2025 and GPQA‑Diamond further test long-horizon and graduate-level reasoning</cite>.

How these benchmarks are evaluated (protocols and metrics)

- Math and logic: Chain-of-thought prompting is widely used; answers are parsed (numeric or boxed expressions) and scored by Exact Match (EM) or numeric proximity. <cite id="382b0788-3">Chain-of-thought is adopted for GSM8K and MATH500; performance is measured by Exact Match with rule-based parsers extracting numeric answers</cite> <cite id="382b0788-4">For MATH500 and AIME2024, boxed expressions are used for answer extraction; for GSM8K, numeric matching follows standard conventions</cite>. 
- Code: Functional correctness under hidden unit tests is typically Pass@1; some studies explicitly distinguish zero-shot (HumanEval) vs few-shot (MBPP). <cite id="382b0788-3">Pass@1 measures the percentage of problems solved on first attempt; HumanEval (zero-shot handwritten) vs MBPP (few-shot) test different coding regimes</cite>. 
- Science/commonsense: Multiple-choice accuracy is standard; harder variants increase option counts (e.g., MMLU‑Pro 10-way) to reduce guessing, and some include abstention/uncertainty penalties to discourage spurious confidence. <cite id="52760b4f-1">MMLU‑Pro uses 10 options per question to reduce guessability and filters low-difficulty items; evaluation emphasizes standardized prompting and reasoning robustness</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-0">GPQA Diamond questions are designed to be difficult even outside specialty; human accuracy near 65%, with 4-choice MC evaluation</cite>. 
- Behavior and trace-level analysis: Beyond accuracy, surveys and methods analyze reasoning dynamics (e.g., step quality, self-correction), prompting strategies, and failure modes. <cite id="b453ef15-3">Surveys investigate how LLMs behave across reasoning tasks and prevalent evaluation methods that analyze reasoning behavior beyond final accuracy</cite>. 

Trends: saturation, long-horizon stress tests, and inference-time methods

- Saturation at the top: Frontier models achieve near-perfect results across many existing benchmarks, prompting a shift toward longer-horizon, adversarially filtered, and web-offline-hard settings. <cite id="b453ef15-1">Leaderboards are increasingly saturated by GPT‑4/Claude/Qwen‑series models achieving near‑perfect results, underscoring the need for more challenging benchmarks</cite>. 
- Long-horizon stressors: Math/olympiad/AIME and GPQA‑Diamond are used to probe multi-step derivations, domain transfer, and resistance to external search. <cite id="382b0788-0">AIME 2024/2025 require final integer answers and stress long-horizon reasoning under high difficulty; GPQA‑Diamond tests generalization beyond math</cite>. 
- Inference-time scaling: Methods like extra time/computation and self-consistency can raise accuracy on math/coding benchmarks, and recent work probes whether similar gains hold in linguistic/pattern puzzles. <cite id="b453ef15-2">Inference-time scaling methods improve math/coding by allocating more time and enabling self-correction; researchers now test whether these methods help on Linguistics Olympiad–style puzzles</cite>. 

Robustness, contamination, and behavior-aware evaluation

- Contamination-resistant design: Harder variants reduce guessing (10-way MMLU‑Pro), curate expert-vetted hard items (GPQA‑Diamond), and even require abstention to avoid trivial recall. <cite id="52760b4f-1">MMLU‑Pro reduces guessability with 10 options and filters low-difficulty items; GPQA uses accuracy plus abstention to stress advanced scientific reasoning beyond memorization</cite>. 
- Robustness and evaluation beyond accuracy: Newer surveys emphasize analyzing reasoning behavior, not just final labels, and propose taxonomies of evaluation methods (e.g., trace analysis, self-evaluation, adversarial probes). <cite id="b453ef15-3">Surveys argue for evaluating LLM reasoning behavior across tasks and provide taxonomies of prevalent evaluation methods beyond task accuracy</cite>. 
- Hard tail and open-ended reasoning: BBEH (from BIG‑Bench Hard) and newer R‑Zero selections target long‑tail reasoning where LLMs historically fall short; multimodal puzzle/olympiad suites aim to capture holistic, abstract problem solving. <cite id="b453ef15-4">MMLU‑Pro, SuperGPQA, and BBEH are used to measure complex reasoning across disciplines and expert-level domains</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-0">HEMM, SciBench, and Olympiad‑Bench target abstract, open-ended reasoning not well covered by earlier benchmarks</cite>. 

Concrete examples and emerging suites (2023–2025)

- R‑Zero’s hard set: MMLU‑Pro, SuperGPQA (285 disciplines, unsearchable), and BBEH (distilled from BIG‑Bench Hard) are used together to stress long-tail reasoning, with EM/Pass@1 reporting following established leaderboards. <cite id="b453ef15-4">MMLU‑Pro, SuperGPQA (unsearchable, 285 disciplines), and BBEH are evaluated for generalization of reasoning; EM accuracy is reported via greedy decoding under a standardized setup</cite>. 
- Multimodal and puzzle-style: PuzzleWorld argues that few benchmarks address abstract, open-ended problems and highlights HEMM, SciBench, MMMU/MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench as covering visual, spatial, analogical, and social reasoning across academic/real-world contexts. <cite id="b453ef15-0">Few benchmarks address abstract, open-ended problems; HEMM, SciBench, MMMU/MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench are designed for multimodal, academic/real-world reasoning</cite>. 
- Behavior/trace analysis: Work on reasoning traces and trajectory analyses spans GPQA‑Diamond, TheoremQA, MMLU‑Pro, and ARC‑Challenge to study step-level reasoning and uncertainty. <cite id="52760b4f-2">Graduate-level evaluations include GPQA Diamond, TheoremQA, MMLU‑Pro, and ARC‑Challenge, enabling analyses of multi-step scientific and commonsense reasoning</cite>. 

Practical guidance

- What to use when: 
  - Math/logic progress: GSM8K (entry point), MATH500/AIME for harder long-horizon derivations; evaluate with CoT and EM via numeric parsing. <cite id="382b0788-0">GSM8K and MATH500 provide complementary difficulty; AIME further stresses long-horizon reasoning</cite> <cite id="382b0788-3">CoT plus EM parsing is standard for math reasoning</cite>. 
  - Science/commonsense: MMLU-Pro (10-way, harder) and GPQA‑Diamond (expert-curated, web-resistant) to assess knowledge-grounded reasoning and reduce guessing. <cite id="52760b4f-1">MMLU‑Pro’s 10-way design and filtering increase difficulty and robustness</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-0">GPQA‑Diamond’s expert-authored questions and ~65% human accuracy make it a stringent science test</cite>. 
  - Code/tool-use: HumanEval and MBPP for unit-test correctness (Pass@1), complemented by LiveCodeBench for broader coding scenarios. <cite id="382b0788-3">Pass@1 and distinction between zero-shot vs few-shot coding regimes</cite> <cite id="382b0788-2">Live-CodeBench expands code reasoning beyond classic datasets</cite>. 
  - Multimodal/creative/olympiad-style: HEMM/SciBench/MMMU‑Pro/Olympiad‑Bench for abstract, cross-discipline reasoning; consider Linguistics Olympiad puzzles to probe pattern systems and inference-time scaling resilience. <cite id="b453ef15-0">HEMM, SciBench, MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench cover abstract, multimodal reasoning</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-2">Linguistics Olympiad tasks expose LLM weaknesses that inference-time scaling may or may not remedy</cite>. 
- Interpreting scores: Expect leaderboard saturation at the top; look for per-subject breakdowns, trace-level diagnostics, and uncertainty behavior. <cite id="b453ef15-1">Leaderboard scores are increasingly saturated by frontier models, motivating harder benchmarks</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-3">Surveys advocate evaluating reasoning behavior and dynamics beyond single-number accuracy</cite>. 

Bottom line
There is a rich, growing set of reasoning benchmarks for LLMs, spanning math/logic (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME), science/commonsense (MMLU‑Pro, GPQA‑Diamond), code/tool-use (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and multimodal/olympiad-style (HEMM, SciBench, Olympiad‑Bench), with evaluation protocols that include chain-of-thought with exact-match parsing, unit-test pass rates, and multiple-choice with increased option counts to reduce guessing. <cite id="382b0788-0">GSM8K, MATH500, and AIME constitute math-heavy long-horizon reasoning suites</cite> <cite id="52760b4f-0">MMLU‑Pro and GPQA‑Diamond raise difficulty and discriminative power for academic and scientific reasoning</cite> <cite id="382b0788-3">Standard protocols include CoT-based EM for math and Pass@1 for code</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-0">HEMM, SciBench, MMMU‑Pro, MMT‑Bench, and Olympiad‑Bench target abstract, multimodal reasoning gaps</cite>. As models saturate older leaderboards, researchers increasingly rely on harder, unsearchable, and open-ended benchmarks to measure genuine reasoning progress and robustness. <cite id="b453ef15-1">Saturation at the top motivates more challenging benchmarks</cite> <cite id="b453ef15-4">MMLU‑Pro, SuperGPQA, and BBEH exemplify recent shifts toward expert-vetted, unsearchable, long-tail reasoning tests</cite>.

Title: PuzzleWorld: A Benchmark for Multimodal, Open-Ended Reasoning in Puzzlehunts
Snippet: Large Language Model (LLM) Reasoning. LLMs have demonstrated remarkable emergent capabilities, often matching or even surpassing human performance across a wide range of tasks (Street et al., 2024). Notably, models such as GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023) and Claude (Anthropic, 2025) have achieved strong results not only on traditional NLP benchmarks-like question answering, summarization, and translation (Widyassari et al., 2022;Soares & Parreiras, 2020;Singh et al., 2017), but also in more complex domains such as mathematical reasoning, programming, and logical deduction (Ahn et al., 2024;Jiang et al., 2024;Lam et al., 2024). These abilities suggest that LLMs are beginning to exhibit general-purpose reasoning skills, making them increasingly relevant to both academic research and practical applications. However, despite these impressive capabilities, understanding the full extent and limitations of LLM reasoning remains a crucial open question, underscoring the need for benchmarks that rigorously assess their capability for flexible, holistic reasoning (Mondorf & Plank, 2024;Chang et al., 2024). 

Reasoning Benchmarks. Numerous reasoning benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate various cognitive skills, including visual mathematical reasoning (Lu et al., 2024), spatial understanding (Wang et al., 2024a), analogical reasoning (Yiu et al., 2024), and social reasoning (Li et al., 2025;Mathur et al., 2025). However, few have addressed abstract, open-ended problems that demand holistic reasoning. HEMM (Liang et al., 2024a), SciBench (Wang et al., 2024b), MMMU (Yue et al., 2024a), MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024b), MMT-Bench (Ying et al., 2024), andOlympiad-Bench (He et al., 2024) test multimodal reasoning across various disciplines in academic and realworld contexts.
</snippet>
<snippet id=b453ef15-1>
Title: CLR-Bench: Evaluating Large Language Models in College-level Reasoning
Snippet: In recent years, the development of various benchmarks has significantly improved the evaluation of large language models (LLMs) from multiple task perspectives. General benchmarks like MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024a), GLUE (Wang et al., 2021), Su-perGLUE (Sarlin et al., 2020), CommonSenseQA (Talmor et al., 2018), BIG-Bench (Srivastava et al., 2022), and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC-Challenge) (Clark et al., 2018) have played a pivotal role in advancing the understanding of language, reasoning, and question-answering tasks, leading to more specialized and comprehensive assessments. More recent benchmarks, such as BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), further enhance the evaluation of model comprehension and complex reasoning abilities. Task-specific benchmarks like HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) have broadened the evaluation landscape, covering diverse areas and expanding the scope of LLM evaluation. 

To facilitate performance comparisons between LLMs, platforms like the OpenLLM Leaderboard (Aidar Myrzakhan, 2024) and OpenCompass (Contributors, 2023) have been established. However, as LLMs evolve rapidly, leaderboard scores are becoming increasingly saturated at the top. Models such as GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023), Claude-3 (Anthropic, 2023b), and open-source models like the Qwen (Yang et al., 2024) series are achieving near-perfect results across various benchmarks. This trend underscores the need for more challenging benchmarks to push the limits of LLM capabilities.
</snippet>
<snippet id=b453ef15-2>
Title: Could language models win the International Linguistics Olympiad?
Snippet: In 2025, OpenAI and Google announced that their large language models (LLMs) would have received gold medals in that year's International Mathematics Olympiad (IMO), a global mathematics competition for secondary students, by answering five of the six competition questions correctly (Huang and Yang, 2025). This is reflective of the growing reasoning capability of stateof-the-art LLMs, which have been shown to perform extremely well on arithmetic and coding benchmarks (Guo et al., 2025;Comanici et al., 2025). This strong performance on these benchmarks has been aided further by the development of inference-time scaling methods, where the models are allocated greater time and computational resources to produce outputs, allowing the models to self-correct, check for self-consistency, and hence improve performance (Muennighoff et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2023). 

Contrastingly, LLMs perform significantly worse on benchmarks based on the International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL), the IMO's linguistic counterpart, designed to test secondary students' ability to recognise and apply patterns in real-world, often lesser-known languages (Chi et al., 2024;Bean et al., 2024). In light of this, there has been growing interest in measuring and improving the ability of LLMs to solve these problems, across the various puzzle formats present in the Linguistics Olympiad papers (see Figure 1 and Appendix A for examples of these formats) (Zhu et al., 2025;Choudhary et al., 2025). 

This naturally leads to the question of whether inference-time scaling methods, which have seen success in other domains but are as yet largely untested in the linguistic puzzle space, can provide similar value when applied to this benchmark (Snell et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2023;Yao et al., 2023). Accordingly, we aim to optimise the 'extraction' of reasoning from these models, to hence determine whether their poor performance is remediable at inference-time, or is reflective of a true deficiency in the specialised reasoning modes required for this domain.
</snippet>

Title: Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating the Reasoning Behavior of Large Language Models - A Survey
Snippet: Specifically, we address the following research questions: 

RQ1: How do current LLMs behave across diverse reasoning tasks? RQ2: What are the prevalent evaluation methods employed to assess the reasoning behavior of large language models? 

Other Surveys. While various surveys on reasoning within large language models have emerged in recent years (Huang & Chang, 2023;Yu et al., 2024;Sun et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2023;Qiao et al., 2023;Chu et al., 2023;Mialon et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2024;Ahn et al., 2024), these studies predominantly focus on techniques that seek to enhance or benchmark the performance of LLMs on downstream reasoning tasks. However, there seems to exist no review of work yet that assesses the reasoning behavior of LLMs, rather than their final task performance. Hence, the contributions of this survey are as follows: (i) To the best of our knowledge, we present the first comprehensive review of literature that evaluates LLMbased reasoning beyond task accuracy, offering deeper insights into the models' reasoning behavior, and (ii) we suggest a taxonomy that categorizes prevalent evaluation methods designed to analyze the reasoning dynamics of LLMs.
</snippet>

Title: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data
Snippet: To test for the generalization of reasoning ability, we evaluate on the following challenging benchmarks: 

• MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024): An enhanced version of the MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) benchmark, featuring a more challenging suite of multi-task questions designed to provide a stricter evaluation of language model capabilities. 

• SuperGPQA (Du et al., 2025): A large-scale benchmark focused on graduate-level reasoning. 

It comprises questions across 285 distinct disciplines that have been verified as unsearchable on the web, thereby isolating true reasoning ability from simple knowledge recall. 

• BBEH (shoaa kazemi et al., 2025): This benchmark builds upon the foundation of BIG-Bench Hard (Suzgun et al., 2023) by incorporating a new selection of tasks specifically engineered to be more difficult, thus providing a more accurate measure of complex reasoning skills. 

For this category, we follow the experimental setup, prompts, and evaluation codes from (Ma et al., 2025), reporting Exact Match (EM) accuracy obtained via greedy decoding.

GPQA-Diamond. GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al., 2023] is a carefully curated subset of the GPQA benchmark, consisting of 198 multiple-choice questions in biology, chemistry, and physics. BBEH. BBEH (Big-Bench Esports Hard) [Kazemi et al., 2025] is a distilled subset of BIG-bench, focusing on tasks where language models historically fail to reach human-level performance. BBEH serves as a critical measure of a model's capacity to tackle "long-tail" reasoning problems beyond patterns typically found in training corpora.

Title: PuzzleWorld: A Benchmark for Multimodal, Open-Ended Reasoning in Puzzlehunts
Snippet: Large Language Model (LLM) Reasoning. LLMs have demonstrated remarkable emergent capabilities, often matching or even surpassing human performance across a wide range of tasks (Street et al., 2024). Notably, models such as GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023) and Claude (Anthropic, 2025) have achieved strong results not only on traditional NLP benchmarks-like question answering, summarization, and translation (Widyassari et al., 2022;Soares & Parreiras, 2020;Singh et al., 2017), but also in more complex domains such as mathematical reasoning, programming, and logical deduction (Ahn et al., 2024;Jiang et al., 2024;Lam et al., 2024). These abilities suggest that LLMs are beginning to exhibit general-purpose reasoning skills, making them increasingly relevant to both academic research and practical applications. However, despite these impressive capabilities, understanding the full extent and limitations of LLM reasoning remains a crucial open question, underscoring the need for benchmarks that rigorously assess their capability for flexible, holistic reasoning (Mondorf & Plank, 2024;Chang et al., 2024). 

Reasoning Benchmarks. Numerous reasoning benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate various cognitive skills, including visual mathematical reasoning (Lu et al., 2024), spatial understanding (Wang et al., 2024a), analogical reasoning (Yiu et al., 2024), and social reasoning (Li et al., 2025;Mathur et al., 2025). However, few have addressed abstract, open-ended problems that demand holistic reasoning. HEMM (Liang et al., 2024a), SciBench (Wang et al., 2024b), MMMU (Yue et al., 2024a), MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024b), MMT-Bench (Ying et al., 2024), andOlympiad-Bench (He et al., 2024) test multimodal reasoning across various disciplines in academic and realworld contexts.

Title: CLR-Bench: Evaluating Large Language Models in College-level Reasoning

To provide a comprehensive overview of the experimental setup, we summarize the key statistics and evaluation protocols for the four benchmarks used in this study: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021b), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021a), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021a), and MATH500 (a representative subset of 500 problems sampled from the original MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021a)). These datasets are selected to evaluate the model's performance in high-precision reasoning and code generation tasks. 

Mathematical Reasoning. For GSM8K and MATH500, we adopt the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting method to elicit multi-step reasoning. The model's performance is measured by Exact Match accuracy. We use a standardized rule-based parser to extract numerical answers from the generated trajectories. MATH500, as a representative subset of the MATH benchmark, involves competition-level problems requiring significantly higher logical consistency. 

Code Generation. For HumanEval and MBPP, we evaluate the functional correctness of the generated Python scripts. We report the Pass@1 metric, which signifies the percentage of problems where the first generated solution passes all hidden unit tests. While HumanEval focuses on zero-shot hand-written problems, MBPP tests the model's ability to solve basic programming tasks with a few-shot setup. (b) Ablation on Dream-7B. 

Figure 9. Radar charts illustrating the performance on GSM8K. STaRR (T+S) consistently expands the performance envelope. Note that relying solely on temporal signals leads to a higher risk of decoding errors due to threshold decay for persistent masked tokens.

documents.snippet: A.2.1 Benchmark Details. We evaluate on four math reasoning benchmarks and one out-of-domain (OOD) science QA benchmark. Table 6 summarizes dataset sizes and answer formats. GSM8K. GSM8K consists of grade-school math word problems with short numerical answers [6]. We train on the GSM8K training split and report results on its official test split. MATH500. MATH is a challenging competition-level math dataset spanning multiple subjects (e.g., algebra, geometry, number theory) [14]. We report results on MATH500, a 500-problem evaluation subset commonly used to assess harder mathematical reasoning. Compared with GSM8K, MATH500 typically requires longer, multistep derivations. AIME 2024/2025. We evaluate on the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) problems from years 2024 and 2025. AIME problems are competition-style and require producing a final integer answer in [0, 999] (as provided by the official problem sets and solutions). These benchmarks further stress long-horizon reasoning and robustness under high difficulty. GPQA-Diamond. To test OOD generalization beyond math, we evaluate on the GPQA-Diamond subset [28], which contains the hardest graduate-level science questions in GPQA.

Title: Probing the Trajectories of Reasoning Traces in Large Language Models
Snippet: Datasets GPQA Diamond. We use the GPQA Diamond dataset [42], a challenging benchmark of 198 graduate-level multiplechoice questions in biology, chemistry, and physics. Questions were written by domain experts and validated to be difficult even for experts outside their specialty, with human expert accuracy around 65%. Each question has four answer choices (A-D). GPQA Diamond represents the highest-quality subset of the broader GPQA dataset, selected for question clarity and expert agreement. 

MMLU-Pro. We use the MMLU-Pro dataset [43], an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark containing 12,032 questions across 14 subject categories spanning STEM (biology, chemistry, computer science, engineering, math, physics), humanities (history, law, philosophy), and social sciences (business, economics, health, psychology, other). Unlike the original MMLU with four answer choices, MMLU-Pro expands to ten choices (A-J) per question, reducing the effectiveness of random guessing and increasing difficulty. Questions were filtered to remove trivial items and augmented with more challenging, reasoning-focused problems.

Title: Deep Research as Rubric for Reinforcement Learning
Snippet: GPQA. GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A) is a high-difficulty multiple-choice benchmark authored by domain experts in biology, chemistry, and physics. The questions are explicitly designed to be challenging for non-experts even with internet access, while remaining answerable by specialists. The benchmark provides multiple subsets, including a high-quality expert-consensus subset (GPQA-Diamond). Evaluation is performed using accuracy and abstention rate, serving as a stress test for advanced scientific reasoning beyond memorization. 

MMLU-Pro. MMLU-Pro is an enhanced version of the original MMLU benchmark, designed to improve discriminative power and robustness. It contains 12,032 multiple-choice questions across 14 domains, with each question expanded to 10 answer options to reduce guessability. Low-difficulty and noisy items are filtered using model-based screening and expert review. Evaluation focuses on accuracy under standardized prompting, with the benchmark emphasizing reasoning robustness and reduced sensitivity to prompt variations.

Title: Empirical Characterization of Inference-Time Elicited Probability Transformations in Large Language Models
Snippet: We evaluate across four graduate-level benchmarks spanning diverse reasoning domains: 

• GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2023): 198 graduate-level science questions (physics, chemistry, biology) 

• TheoremQA (Chen et al., 2023): 800 theoremapplication problems in mathematics 

• MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024): 490 multisubject reasoning problems with 10 answer options

Title: ALIVE: Awakening LLM Reasoning via Adversarial Learning and Instructive Verbal Evaluation
Snippet: MMLU-Pro. MMLU-Pro [Wang et al., 2024b] is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, developed to address the saturation of performance on general knowledge tasks. It expands both the number of answer choices per question and the complexity of reasoning across 14 diverse subjects. By lowering the probability of success through random guessing, MMLU-Pro provides a more rigorous evaluation of a model's academic knowledge and reasoning abilities. 

GPQA-Diamond. GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al., 2023] is a carefully curated subset of the GPQA benchmark, consisting of 198 multiple-choice questions in biology, chemistry, and physics. The questions span advanced undergraduate to postgraduate difficulty levels. Each item was selected such that domain experts answered correctly while the majority of non-experts did not, ensuring both high discriminative power and quality. 

SuperGPQA. SuperGPQA [Team et al., 2025b] is a high-difficulty benchmark designed to evaluate expert-level knowledge across a wide range of scientific and technical domains. Building on GPQA's methodology, it spans a broader set of specialized subjects and demands deep domain expertise. The tasks are crafted to challenge even human experts, offering a rigorous assessment of large language models' capabilities in advanced scientific reasoning. 

BBEH. BBEH (Big-Bench Esports Hard) [Kazemi et al., 2025] is a distilled subset of BIG-bench, focusing on tasks where language models historically fail to reach human-level performance. It spans linguistic, logical, and creative challenges requiring nuanced understanding and multi-step reasoning. BBEH serves as a critical measure of a model's capacity to tackle "long-tail" reasoning problems beyond patterns typically found in training corpora.

Title: RAISE: Enhancing Scientific Reasoning in LLMs via Step-by-Step Retrieval
Snippet: B.1 Dataset Details GPQA [29] This dataset consists of physics, biology, and chemistry questions written by domain experts. We use GPQA diamond subset, which consist of 198 high-quality questions selected based on human performance. Specifically, this subset includes questions that both experts answer correctly while the majority of non-experts fail to solve. Each question typically demands multistep reasoning, precise formula manipulation, and access to external scientific facts (e.g., physical constants, definitions). Due to its alignment with our target setting, GPQA serves as the primary evaluation benchmark throughout our experiments. 

For GPQA, the original dataset does not include standardized multiple-choice labeled as (A), (B), (C) and (D). To ensure consistency during evaluation, we proprocessed each question by randomly shuffling the correct answer along with the three distractors, and assigning them uniformly to choice labels (A) through (D). 

SuperGPQA [32] SuperGPQA is a large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate graduate-level reasoning across 13 disciplines, 72 fields, and 285 graduate-level disciplines. In alignment with the scientific reasoning focus of our work, we select science and engineering domains for evaluation. Each domain is further divided by three difficulty levels(easy, medium, and hard). To reduce computational overhead while maintaining consistency, we randomly sample 199 questions per subset using a fixed seed (42). Specifically, our experiments include 199 examples each from science-hard, science-middle, and engineering-hard subsets. 

MMLU [6,36] The MMLU benchmark covers a wide range of subjects across multiple domains. 

For out experiments, we focus on STEM and Professional categories. The STEM contains universitylevel science and engineering subjects such as college mathematics and computer science, while the Professional category covers specialized fields that typically require professional training or advanced education, including law, medicine, and chemistry. We specifically select three subsets: college chemistry from MMLU-STEM and professional chemistry and biology from MMLU-Pro. These subsets are chosen to evaluate our method's ability to perform scientific reasoning in both academic and professional contexts involving complex domain knowledge.

The question could ask which type of reasoning a specific benchmark family measures, forcing the system to reason about benchmark design rather than just list names.

harder.why_harder: The question requires the system to: (1) identify the cognitive reasoning construct ARC purportedly measures (e.g., commonsense physical reasoning, analogical reasoning, scientific reasoning); (2) analyze whether ARC's multiple-choice format and question types actually isolate that construct or conflate it with world knowledge retrieval, reading comprehension, or elimination strategies; (3) evaluate validation evidence about what the benchmark correlates with. A survey-strong system can retrieve papers describing ARC as 'reasoning,' but determining what reasoning type it isolates and whether the design succeeds requires analyzing task structure against cognitive constructs—a synthesis challenge.

Summary
ARC benchmarks (ARC/ARC-AGI/ARC-C/E) are designed to probe abstract reasoning—specifically, few-shot induction of latent transformation rules over 2D grids and the flexible application of those rules to novel inputs. Their core cognitive construct aligns with “fluid” or System 2–like abilities—compositionality, symbolic manipulation, analogy-making, and generalization from sparse demonstrations—while explicitly constraining reliance on external knowledge, large training corpora, and statistical overfitting to surface reasoning rather than idiosyncratic pattern matching. However, empirical analyses show that performance on ARC-style tasks can conflate perceptual and reasoning limits, exploit statistical regularities, and depend on test-time compute and working-memory/sequential demands, so the tasks do not fully isolate abstract reasoning from important confounds. <cite id="48d659a2-0">ARC-AGI tasks are few-shot grid-transformation problems where a solver infers a rule from 3–5 input–output grids and applies it to held-out tests</cite><cite id="48d659a2-1">ARC-AGI was created to distinguish genuine reasoning from pattern matching and sits alongside benchmarks like Raven’s Progressive Matrices but requires open-ended rule induction rather than multiple-choice pattern recognition</cite><cite id="48d659a2-2">Systems now reach 93% on ARC-AGI-1 yet collapse to 13% on ARC-AGI-3, indicating limits in compositional generalization that are orthogonal to broad knowledge breadth</cite><cite id="48d659a2-3">ARC emphasizes abstract rule inference, compositional reasoning, and analogymaking under constraints that forbid large datasets or handcrafted features, mirroring System 2 cognition</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">ARC-AGI is designed to require a small set of priors and can theoretically be solved without language models, positioning it as a reasoning and abstraction benchmark</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-2">ARC-C/E are framed as challenging multiple-choice questions requiring logical inference, synthesis, and deductive reasoning</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-3">ARC tasks align with the Language of Thought Hypothesis’s emphasis on logical coherence, compositionality, and productivity</cite><cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2 explicitly targets compositional complexity with multi-step transformations and control-flow dependencies that resist brute-force search</cite>.

What cognitive construct does ARC measure?
- Inductive abstraction over visual patterns: ARC/ARC-AGI present 2D grids with 3–5 exemplars and a single test input; success requires hypothesizing a concise transformation rule and producing an exact output grid. The benchmark explicitly forbids training on task-specific data and discourages handcrafted features to force inductive abstraction rather than memorization. <cite id="48d659a2-0">Given a number of input–output example grids (typically 3–5), a solver must infer the rule and produce the exact output grid for a held-out test input</cite><cite id="48d659a2-0">Evaluations use a public development set and a disjoint private set to reduce contamination</cite><cite id="48d659a2-3">No prior training on the tasks is allowed, and the use of large datasets or handcrafted features is explicitly discouraged</cite>.
- System 2–style reasoning: ARC emphasizes compositional generalization, symbolic manipulation, and analogy-making from minimal demonstrations—capabilities often associated with slow, effortful reasoning. <cite id="48d659a2-3">Solving ARC demands inference of abstract rules and application to unseen examples, requiring compositional reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and analogymaking central to System 2</cite>.
- Fluid intelligence alignment: ARC-AGI is positioned as a probe of fluid reasoning/abstract reasoning that resists statistical overfitting and rewards adaptivity and reuse across novel structures. <cite id="48d659a2-2">ARC-AGI is a key benchmark for fluid intelligence, with consistent 2–3× drops across versions across paradigms, indicating fundamental limits in compositional generalization; models vary widely in score and cost, and test-time adaptation emerges as critical</cite><cite id="48d659a2-1">ARC-AGI was designed as a diagnostic to separate genuine reasoning from sophisticated pattern matching</cite>.
- Relation to classic reasoning: ARC’s grid-based format is often compared to Raven’s Progressive Matrices; both target abstract visual reasoning, but ARC’s open-ended rule induction and single-test-input design require synthesis of transformations rather than selection among multiple choices. <cite id="48d659a2-1">Visual reasoning benchmarks like RAVEN share surface similarity but emphasize pattern recognition over transformation synthesis; ARC-AGI’s open-ended generation requirement creates different solution constraints</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">ARC resembles Raven’s Progressive Matrices with input–output grids and transformation rules to infer</cite>.

Does ARC isolate abstract reasoning—or does it conflate with other capacities?
- Evidence that ARC isolates core reasoning processes:
  - Design constraints minimize knowledge and feature engineering, pushing solutions toward abstraction and compositional generalization rather than lookup or statistical memorization. <cite id="48d659a2-3">No prior training is allowed and use of large datasets or handcrafted features is discouraged, forcing abstract rule induction</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">Tasks are carefully constructed to require a small set of priors and are designed to be solvable without language models</cite>.
  - ARC-AGI-1/2 show large performance cliffs across versions that correlate with increased compositional depth and control-flow dependencies, consistent with limits in fluid reasoning rather than broad knowledge. <cite id="48d659a2-2">Performance degrades from 93% on ARC-AGI-1 to 68.8% on ARC-AGI-2 and 13% on ARC-AGI-3; humans remain near-perfect, highlighting fundamental compositional generalization limits</cite><cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2 increases difficulty via multi-step transformations where outcomes depend step-by-step and introduces subtle distinctions that resist brute-force search</cite>.
- Evidence that ARC conflates multiple capacities (confounds it does not fully isolate):
  - Perception bottlenecks dominate performance gaps: a controlled two-stage pipeline that decouples description (perception) from rule induction/appplication shows that the dominant source of error is perception; end-to-end gains largely reflect better perceptual descriptions rather than stronger abstract reasoning. <cite id="69430ee1-2">A two-stage pipeline that separates image-to-language description (perception) from model-based reasoning across Mini-ARC, ACRE, and Bongard-LOGO finds the perception capability is the dominant factor underlying performance gaps; roughly 80% of model failures stem from perception errors, indicating ARC-style benchmarks conflate perceptual and reasoning challenges</cite><cite id="69430ee1-0">Vision-language synergy improves ARC by leveraging global 2D structural understanding from vision and precise element-wise processing from text, underscoring that visual reasoning complements textual reasoning</cite>.
  - Human performance and difficulty are not aligned with AI: large-scale H-ARC shows task difficulty varies widely for humans and AI, with AI sometimes surging on human-difficult tasks and faltering on human-easy ones, suggesting reliance on surface features rather than abstract reasoning. <cite id="48d659a2-1">H-ARC shows task difficulty for humans does not correlate with difficulty for AI; high AI performance on tasks humans find difficult, combined with AI failure on tasks humans find easy, indicates reliance on surface features rather than abstract reasoning</cite>.
  - Statistical regularities and test-time compute can substitute for reasoning: analyses of ARC-AGI winners reveal exploitable regularities and vulnerability to brute-force search with sufficient test-time compute, implying performance reflects search and data scaling rather than principled compositional reasoning. <cite id="48d659a2-2">Successful ARC-AGI systems needed hundreds of thousands of synthetic examples to reach 24% on ARC-AGI-2, confirming that reasoning remains knowledge-bound; test-time adaptation and refinement loops are critical, and compositionality remains unsolved</cite><cite id="48d659a2-4">Tasks exhibit clear difficulty progression and successful systems exploited limited compositional depth, statistical regularities in transformation types, and brute-force vulnerability</cite>.
  - Working memory and sequential planning demands leak into reasoning: ARC-AGI-2 explicitly builds in multi-step, state-dependent transformations that require executing prior steps to predict later outcomes, increasing memory and dependency burden that can mask reasoning deficits. <cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2 requires deeper compositional reasoning with multi-step transformations where the state after step N depends on step N−1, making prediction virtually impossible without sequential execution; control-flow complexity and subtle distinctions resist brute-force search</cite>.
  - Language/tool-use confounds can be decisive: ARC-agency and related agentic ARC-style suites shift the core task toward tool-use and interaction; performance may reflect tool-use skill, interface fluency, and function-calling rather than pure abstract rule induction. <cite id="326b25d4-2">BBEH evaluates multi-step reasoning and tool-augmented problem solving across benchmarks like SWE-Bench and WorkBench, highlighting the confound of tool-use alongside reasoning in agentic settings</cite><cite id="326b25d4-3">Recent enterprise agent benchmarks (e.g., FORCE-Bench) add professional quality dimensions but many prior agent evaluations emphasize function-calling accuracy rather than reasoning quality, illustrating tool-use confounds</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">ARC-AGI is designed to require a small set of priors and can be solved without language models; however, related ARC-style evaluations often introduce language and tool-use demands that weren’t present in the original design</cite>.
- ARC-vision evidence: Some ARC variants explicitly leverage visual reasoning as a complementary modality, reinforcing that vision-language integration, not just abstract rule induction, drives performance. <cite id="69430ee1-0">Vision-language synergy reasoning uses visual rule summarization for global structure and textual manipulation for precise operations, with modality-switch self-correction ensuring visual consistency</cite><cite id="69430ee1-1">ARC resembles Raven’s but with input–output grids encoding a hidden transformation; visual and textual modalities are complementary, and humans often rely on vision, with some patterns evident visually but convoluted in language</cite><cite id="69430ee1-4">EasyARC targets “true visual reasoning” and shows frontier VLMs fail on a simple ARC-inspired benchmark, diagnosing missing visual understanding components</cite>.

Do ARC-agency and ARC-vision better isolate reasoning?
- ARC-vision: By formalizing the interaction between vision and language, ARC-vision-style methods show that abstract reasoning depends on how visual structure is extracted and manipulated. Decoupling perception from reasoning reveals large performance penalties from weak vision, implying that ARC-vision does not isolate abstract reasoning unless perceptual channels are controlled. <cite id="69430ee1-2">Decoupling description (perception) from reasoning shows perception is the dominant bottleneck; ARC-style performance gaps reflect perceptual limitations when reasoning is separated from perception</cite><cite id="69430ee1-0">ARC-vision methods explicitly exploit complementary strengths: vision for global 2D structure and text for element-wise manipulation</cite>.
- ARC-agency: Introducing agency/tool use shifts emphasis from pure abstract induction to interactive planning and function selection. Benchmarks like BBEH and WorkBench demonstrate that tool-use skill and API-calling accuracy can inflate “reasoning” scores independent of abstract inductive ability, suggesting agency evaluations must orthogonalize tool-use fluency from conceptual reasoning. <cite id="326b25d4-2">BBEH and related agent benchmarks evaluate multi-step reasoning together with tool-augmented problem solving, highlighting the confound of tool-use with reasoning</cite><cite id="326b25d4-3">Tool-use and function-calling benchmarks emphasize function-calling accuracy over response quality, underscoring that performance can reflect tool-use rather than pure reasoning</cite>.

What would better isolate the construct?
- Decouple perception and reasoning with perceptually blind baselines: require models to solve via intermediate descriptions or symbolic encodings of visual scenes, with separate modules for description quality and rule induction, and compare to fully end-to-end baselines. <cite id="69430ee1-2">A two-stage pipeline that explicitly separates image-to-language description from rule induction/appplication isolates reasoning from perception and reveals perception as dominant; end-to-end gains overestimate reasoning gains</cite>.
- Control for statistical overfitting and test-time compute: enforce limits on synthetic examples, disallow test-time training, and randomize search space properties; evaluate under compute caps to prevent brute-force dominance. <cite id="48d659a2-2">ARC-AGI winners exploited statistical regularities and needed large synthetic datasets and heavy test-time compute, indicating that knowledge-bound search, not principled compositionality, drove gains</cite><cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2 was designed to expand search spaces and introduce subtle distinctions that resist brute-force enumeration, targeting compositional complexity</cite>.
- Orthogonalize working memory demands: randomize grid sizes, introduce synthetic long dependency chains, and require proofs or intermediate checkpoints that must be preserved across steps to separate memory/sequencing capacity from rule abstraction. <cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2’s multi-step, state-dependent transformations make prediction impossible without executing sequential operations, emphasizing memory and control-flow complexity</cite>.
- Isolate language/tool confounds: provide nonlinguistic interfaces for abstract rule induction (e.g., structured symbolic API), and evaluate with identical tools across models; compare tool-free vs. tool-enabled ARC variants to quantify the added value of agency. <cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">ARC-AGI can be solved without language models, but ARC-style evaluations often introduce language demands; controlling for language/tool demands isolates the abstract reasoning construct</cite><cite id="326b25d4-2">Agent benchmarks that combine reasoning and tool-use confound the two; evaluations should separate tool-use skill from conceptual reasoning</cite>.

Takeaways
- What ARC measures: ARC/ARC-AGI primarily measure abstract inductive reasoning—hypothesizing concise transformation rules from few examples and applying them compositionally to novel 2D grids—designed to reward generalization over memorization and mimic System 2-like cognition. <cite id="48d659a2-0">ARC-AGI presents 3–5 exemplars and a single test input requiring abstract rule induction</cite><cite id="48d659a2-3">Solving ARC requires abstract rule inference, compositional reasoning, and analogymaking under constraints that discourage overfitting</cite><cite id="f0e7f8fd-1">Tasks are constructed to require a small set of priors and can be solved without language models</cite>.
- Isolation vs. confounds: While ARC’s design removes many extraneous cues (no external knowledge), it cannot fully decouple visual perception, statistical structure exploitation, test-time compute, and working-memory/sequential dependencies; ARC-vision and ARC-agency further shift emphasis toward vision-language synergy and tool-use, which can dominate performance unless explicitly controlled. <cite id="69430ee1-2">ARC-style performance gaps largely reflect perception bottlenecks when reasoning is decoupled from vision</cite><cite id="48d659a2-1">AI often succeeds where humans struggle and vice versa on ARC-AGI, indicating surface-feature reliance</cite><cite id="48d659a2-2">Winning ARC-AGI systems relied on large synthetic examples and test-time adaptation, revealing knowledge-bound search</cite><cite id="48d659a2-4">ARC-AGI-2’s design targets compositional complexity to resist brute-force and increase sequential dependencies</cite><cite id="69430ee1-0">ARC-vision methods show complementary vision-language strengths essential for solving ARC</cite>.
- Practical interpretation: ARC-family benchmarks are strong diagnostics of abstract inductive reasoning when paired with perceptually blind, compute-limited, and memory-aware evaluation protocols; as currently administered—especially in ARC-vision/agency variants—they often reflect the interplay of perception, tool-use fluency, and search strategies, so claims of “reasoning” should be calibrated with perceptual-only baselines and tool-use controls. <cite id="69430ee1-2">Perception-then-reasoning pipelines reveal that controlling vision dramatically changes measured “reasoning” performance</cite><cite id="326b25d4-3">Agent benchmarks that emphasize function-calling accuracy over response quality illustrate how tool-use can substitute for reasoning</cite><cite id="48d659a2-2">Test-time adaptation and compute are critical on ARC-AGI, suggesting performance reflects efficiency of skill acquisition rather than pure reasoning</cite>.

Title: DiARC: Distinguishing Positive and Negative Samples Helps Improving ARC-like Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models
Snippet: Dataset and Evaluation. We evaluate on six benchmarks that cover the original ARC setting, its harder successor, and four related ARC-style transfer or additional benchmarks. ARC-AGI-1 (Chollet, 2019) is the original ARC benchmark for fewshot abstract rule induction from grid-based inputoutput examples, and we use its 400-task public evaluation set. ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet et al., 2025) is a harder successor that preserves the same inputoutput format while providing a more challenging test of abstract reasoning and problem solving, and we use its 120-task public evaluation set. MiniARC (Kim et al., 2022) is a compact 5×5 ARC-style benchmark designed to reduce variation in grid size and focus more directly on abductive reasoning. Title: The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning
Snippet: The pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) requires benchmarks that can distinguish genuine reasoning from sophisticated pattern matching. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC-AGI) [Chollet 2019] stands out as such a benchmark, highlighting important limitations about the current state of AI. While humans solve these tasks with near-perfect accuracy, AI systems show dramatic performance variation. Since its 2019 introduction, ARC-AGI has evolved through three progressively more challenging versions. The tasks are few-shot grid-transformation problems. Given a number of input-output example grids (typically 3-5), a solver (system or human) must infer the rule and produce the exact output grid for a held-out test input. To reduce benchmark-specific tuning and contamination, evaluations use a public development/feedback set and a disjoint private (hidden) set for official leaderboard and competition scoring. On ARC-AGI-1, frontier models now exceed 96% accuracy (Gemini 3 Deep Think at $7.17/task), with Opus 4.6 at 93.0% ($1.88/task) and GPT-5.2 Pro at 90.5% ($11.64/task) [ARC Prize Foundation 2025a], the latter representing a 390× efficiency improvement in one year from o3's $4,500/task. However, performance drops on ARC-AGI-2. Gemini 3 Deep Think leads at 84.6% ($13.62/task), while under Kaggle resource constraints the best system (NVARC) achieved only 24% [ARC Prize Foundation 2025b]. On ARC-AGI-3, performance drops further to 13% [Kamradt 2025]. While ARC Prize designed the benchmark to be fully solvable by humans, evaluation studies show that each ARC-AGI-2 task is solved by roughly 75% of individual participants [Chollet et al. 2025b], reflecting task difficulty variation rather than fundamental human limitations. NYU published a study assessing Mechanical Turk workers, which showed an average worker solves 77% of the ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation tasks [ARC Prize Foundation 2025a;LeGris et al. 2024].
</snippet>

Title: The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning
Snippet: ARC-AGI exists within a broader ecosystem of benchmarks attempting to measure aspects of AGI and reasoning capability. Understanding ARC-AGI's relationship to these alternatives clarifies its unique contributions and limitations. 

Broad AGI Evaluation Suites: Big-Bench [Srivastava et al. 2023] and MMLU [Hendrycks et al. 2021a] assess language models across hundreds of diverse tasks spanning mathematics, science, history, and common sense reasoning. These benchmarks measure breadth of acquired knowledge and capabilities, operating in the complementary regime to ARC-AGI's focus on fewshot generalization from minimal data. Large language models achieve >90% on many MMLU categories yet remain below 20% on ARC-AGI-2, demonstrating that knowledge breadth and fluid reasoning represent orthogonal challenges. Our survey focuses exclusively on the latter. 

Visual Reasoning Benchmarks: RAVEN's Progressive Matrices [Zhang et al. 2019] and similar abstract visual reasoning tasks share surface similarity with ARC-AGI's grid-based format. However, RAVEN provides multiple-choice answers and emphasizes pattern recognition over transformation synthesis. While some ARC-AGI techniques transfer to these domains, the open-ended generation requirement in ARC-AGI creates fundamentally different solution constraints. 

Human Baseline Studies: H-ARC [LeGris et al. 2024] provides robust human performance estimates through a large-scale study collecting over 1,700 solution attempts from 316 participants on all 400 ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation tasks. Their findings reveal that task difficulty for humans does not correlate with difficulty for AI systems, suggesting fundamentally different reasoning strategies. This disconnect reinforces ARC-AGI's value as a diagnostic tool: high AI performance on tasks humans find difficult, combined with AI failure on tasks humans find easy, indicates reliance on surface features rather than the abstract reasoning humans employ. 

Interactive and Embodied Environments: BabyAI [Chevalier-Boisvert et al. 2019], NetHack [Küttler et al. 2020], and Crafter [Hafner 2021] evaluate sequential decision-making and long-horizon planning in interactive environments.
</snippet>

Title: The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning
Snippet: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC-AGI) has become a key benchmark for fluid intelligence in AI. This survey presents the first cross-generation analysis of 82 approaches across three benchmark versions and the ARC Prize 2024-2025 competitions. Our central finding is that performance degradation across versions is consistent across all paradigms: program synthesis, neuro-symbolic, and neural approaches all exhibit 2-3x drops from ARC-AGI-1 to ARC-AGI-2, indicating fundamental limitations in compositional generalization. While systems now reach 93.0% on ARC-AGI-1 (Opus 4.6), performance falls to 68.8% on ARC-AGI-2 and 13% on ARC-AGI-3, as humans maintain near-perfect accuracy across all versions. Cost fell 390x in one year (o3's $4,500/task to GPT-5.2's $12/task), although this largely reflects reduced test-time parallelism. Trillion-scale models vary widely in score and cost, while Kaggle-constrained entries (660M-8B) achieve competitive results, aligning with Chollet's thesis that intelligence is skill-acquisition efficiency. Test-time adaptation and refinement loops emerge as critical success factors, while compositional reasoning and interactive learning remain unsolved. ARC Prize 2025 winners needed hundreds of thousands of synthetic examples to reach 24% on ARC-AGI-2, confirming that reasoning remains knowledge-bound. This first release of the ARC-AGI Living Survey captures the field as of February 2026, with updates at https://nimi-ai.com/arc-survey/
</snippet>

Title: System 2 Reasoning for Human-AI Alignment: Generality and Adaptivity via ARC-AGI
Snippet: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) (Chollet 2019) was introduced as a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating AI systems' ability to reason in a human-like way. Each ARC task presents a few pairs of input and output grids, and the model must predict the correct output for a new input grid using only these limited demonstrations. No prior training on the tasks is allowed, and the use of large datasets or handcrafted features is explicitly discouraged. As a result, solving ARC tasks demands the ability to infer abstract rules and apply them flexibly to unseen examples. 

What makes ARC especially challenging is that it is designed to assess cognitive functions that go beyond statistical pattern recognition. The tasks often require compositional reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and analogymaking, which are capabilities central to what psychologists refer to as System 2 reasoning. Models must identify underlying transformations, manipulate high-level concepts, and generalize from sparse data in ways that mirror human reasoning under uncertainty. 

ARC also serves as a practical testbed for measuring the two key dimensions of AGI reasoning emphasized in this paper: generality and adaptivity. Generality is needed because the tasks are diverse and unpredictable; a model must reuse its knowledge flexibly across different settings. Adaptivity is equally essential, as each ARC task introduces new structural rules, and the model must quickly adjust its strategy based on limited examples. Thus, strong performance on ARC indicates not just surface-level pattern matching but the presence of deeper abstraction and flexible reasoning. 

In this paper, we propose that ARC should be viewed not only as a benchmark, but also as a principled microcosm of AGI-level reasoning. Its design integrates the challenges of generality, adaptivity, and symbolic abstraction, all of which are central to System 2 cognition. By explicitly targeting these capacities, ARC enables the evaluation of AI systems that aim to achieve more robust, general-purpose reasoning. Progress on ARC is therefore not only a matter of empirical performance, but a meaningful step toward developing AI systems capable of adaptive, human-aligned intelligence.
</snippet>

Snippet: The ARC-AGI benchmark has evolved through three versions, each addressing limitations revealed by progress on its predecessor while maintaining the core focus on fluid intelligence. Table 1 summarizes the key differences. Each task contains 3-5 input-output demonstration pairs and typically one test input (occasionally two). Tasks exhibit clear difficulty progression: simple uniform transformations (solved by >90% of systems), object-centric operations with geometric transformations (40-60% success rate), and multi-step reasoning requiring abstraction (<10% success rate). 

For five years, ARC-AGI-1 successfully resisted most AI approaches, with performance remaining below 20% until 2024. The ARC Prize 2024 competition, offering $600,000 for surpassing 85% accuracy, catalyzed rapid progress with over 1,430 teams competing. The top open-source system (ARChitects) achieved 53.5% through test-time training, demonstrating that architectural innovations could break the long-standing performance barrier [Kamradt 2025]. However, analysis of successful systems revealed exploitable characteristics: limited compositional depth (most tasks require 1-2 reasoning steps), statistical regularities in transformation types, and vulnerability to brute-force search given sufficient test-time compute. These findings motivated ARC-AGI-2's design [Chollet et al. 2025b]. 

2.3.2 ARC-AGI-2: Targeting Compositional Complexity. Released in March 2025 following OpenAI o3's breakthrough on ARC-AGI-1, this version maintains the same input-output format while significantly increasing difficulty through four targeted enhancements [Chollet 2024;Chollet et al. 2025b]. First, tasks require deeper compositional reasoning through multi-step transformations where the state after step N depends on step N-1, making it virtually impossible to predict outcomes without executing sequential operations. Many tasks require symbolic, context-dependent pattern interpretation and rule application that adds control-flow complexity. Careful construction expands search spaces and introduces subtle distinctions between correct and plausible-but-wrong solutions, resisting brute-force enumeration [Chollet et al. 2025b].

Title: TimeSage-MT: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating Agentic Time Series Reasoning
Snippet: We build both TimeSage-MT and TimeSage because they answer different questions. TimeSage-MT defines the evaluation problem: 240 tasks, 2,680 dialogue turns, 4 levels, 8 domains, reference code, numerical gold, reasoning annotations, and outcome/capability scoring. TimeSage is a reference structured agent system for the same setting. It demonstrates one engineering pattern for combining planning, skills, executable analysis, deterministic validation, and report generation around the benchmark interface. The benchmark does not require future systems to use the TimeSage architecture. Rather, TimeSage is included to make the system-design question concrete: when does a structured skill-and-harness workflow help, and when do simpler direct or code-enabled agents suffice? 

The scope of validity follows from this design. Within the benchmark contract, TimeSage-MT supports rigorous comparison of agentic systems on verifiable, multi-turn time series reasoning. It is not a benchmark for prompt aesthetics, conversational charm, marketing copy, or open-ended creativity, and we advise against interpreting it that way. It also should not be read as a deployment certificate for high-impact settings. A high leaderboard score means that an agent performed well on the released benchmark distribution; it does not remove the need for local validation, human oversight, privacy review, operational fail-safes, or domain-specific safety approval in finance, healthcare, energy, climate, manufacturing, transportation, telecom, or retail. 

The aggregate outcome and capability scores should be treated as summaries, not as the sole object of research. TimeSage-MT is designed so that researchers can move from a leaderboard number to the underlying evidence: per-task scores, per-turn scores, outcome subtracks, capability subchecks, code outputs, tool traces, skill calls, reasoning-graph alignment, and reviewer/audit metadata. The intended workflow is therefore diagnostic. Rather than only chasing a higher benchmark accuracy, researchers should inspect where an agent failed: whether it misread the data, selected the wrong method, configured a parameter incorrectly, forgot an earlier result, broke a dependency chain, accepted a misleading user hint, understated uncertainty, or made an unsupported domain decision.
</snippet>

Title: Counsel: A Meta-Evaluation Dataset for Agentic Tasks
Snippet: As agentic systems tackle increasingly complex multi-step tasks, evaluating their trajectories presents a major bottleneck - human annotation of a single trajectory on popular agentic benchmarks can take hours, making it difficult to scale evaluations for measuring performance or curating training data. This has driven widespread reliance on automated approaches such as LLM-as-a-judge (LLMJ) to critique agents at the process and outcome-levels at scale, however, the soundness of LLMJ critiques often goes unmeasured. Here, we introduce Counsel, the first public dataset of meta-evaluations for agentic tasks. Counsel consists of process-level critiques from open-weight LLMJs on two agent benchmarks: tau-bench (customer support agents) and DA-Code (coding agents), and human meta-evaluations of these critiques. Human annotators label critiques on each flagged error as"spot on","correct location but poor reasoning", or"should not have flagged", achieving reliable inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha of 0.78). The resulting dataset stratifies LLMJ critiques by human alignment across both error location within a trajectory and reasoning quality, serving as valuable data to calibrate, improve, or train LLMJs for agents. Comparing open-weight judges, we find that more capable judge models and more reasoning effort both enabled improved human agreement, with the strongest judge reaching ~88% agreement on location and ~65% on reasoning. Counsel is generated using open-weight models and is permissively licensed for broad community use, which we hope will enable rigorous study and improved alignment of LLM-based evaluators for agentic systems.
</snippet>

Most emphasize task success or capability metrics (e.g., function calling, reasoning, navigation), while our setting adds professional quality dimensions for finance workflows: accuracy, citations, clarity, depth, groundedness, recency, relevance, and structure. We categorize relevant agent benchmarks as follows: 

Interactive Environment Benchmarks. AgentBench Liu et al. [2024], WebShop Yao et al. [2022b], and Science-World Wang et al. [2022] provide diverse simulation environments for agent evaluation. AgentBench spans 8 distinct environments (web browsing, database query, file I/O, etc.); WebShop simulates e-commerce with 1.18 million realworld products; ScienceWorld tests scientific reasoning in interactive scenarios. Interactive Agent-User Benchmarks. τ -Bench Yao et al. Title: Structured Debate Improves Corporate Credit Reasoning in Financial AI
Snippet: This study evaluated two LLM-based automation systems-the Single-Agent System (SAS) and the Popperian Multi-Agent Debate System (PMADS)-for non-financial data analysis in corporate credit evaluation. The findings supported all three hypotheses. First, both systems substantially outperformed human domain experts in work productivity, as reflected by dramatically shorter task completion times. Second, reports generated by the SAS were perceived by credit risk professionals as adequate or neutral in quality, while those produced by the PMADS were perceived as more than adequate. Third, the PMADS was superior to the SAS across most perceived report quality measures, including explanatory adequacy, practical applicability, and usability, while trustworthiness ratings remained comparable between the two systems. 

The combination of neutral or higher perceived quality and drastically reduced task completion time highlights the practical utility of LLM-powered automation for corporate credit assessment. Both systems demonstrated the potential to alleviate the cognitive and temporal burdens associated with manual report generation, indicating that automation can complement expert judgment rather than replace it. The PMADS, in particular, showed promise as a viable analytical assistant in credit evaluation, as its perceived report quality and usability exceeded neutral benchmarks, suggesting that users found its reasoning coherent and its interface operationally acceptable for real-world workflows. 

The superior reasoning quality of the PMADS over the SAS can be attributed to its debate protocol, which formalizes analysis as a structured process of argumentation. This design accords with the argumentative theory of reasoning (Mercier & Sperber, 2011), which posits that reasoning quality improves when claims are subject to critique rather than produced in isolation. By organizing analysis into sequential stages that require claims to be evidenced, evaluated, and revised, the protocol filters unsupported assumptions and prevents premature closure during inference. Consistent with recent multi-agent research, structured critique and procedural constraints have been shown to enhance reasoning stability and factual reliability by mitigating coordination failures and conversational drift (Gao et al., 2025;Jin et al., 2025).

Title: Think Visually, Reason Textually: Vision-Language Synergy in ARC
Snippet: The core of this work lies in integrating visual thinking into ARC-AGI tasks to use the complementary strengths of different modalities. While existing approaches treat ARC-AGI as a pure text task, we argue that visual and textual modalities excel at different aspects of the reasoning process. Visual thinking provides global perception and 2D structural understanding that text-centric reasoning lacks, while textual thinking enables precise element-wise processing and manipulation. 

To this end, we propose two core methods for ARC-AGI (Fig. 3): a) Vision-Language Synergy Reasoning (VLSR) and b) Modality-Switch Self-Correction (MSSC). VLSR summarizes rules from exemplar matrices in the visual modality and then applies the inferred rule to the test input in the text modality. MSSC verifies the textual output by re-encoding it as an image to assess visual consistency with the examples; if inconsistent, it triggers another textual pass with targeted feedback.

Title: EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning
Snippet: The ARC challenge introduced by Chollet [4] is designed as a benchmark for abstract reasoning robust to memorization. It resembles Raven's Progressive Matrices where a matrix of figures are provided and the test taker has to fill in the last missing figure. However, in the ARC setting we instead have a number of examples consisting of input and output grids which entail a hidden transformation rule between them. In order to demonstrate that the correct transformation rule was found, the test taker then gets one or multiple test input grids and constructs the output grid which is held against a ground truth. [10] demonstrate that these two modes of reasoning are complementary for solving the ARC challenge. Motivated by this, we investigate whether visual reasoning can complement existing approaches to solving ARC problems. This motivation stems from the observation that humans primarily rely on vision to solve ARC problems. Some patterns become evident in the visual domain but could appear convoluted when described through lengthy natural language representations of the grid.

Title: Your Reasoning Benchmark May Not Test Reasoning: Revealing Perception Bottleneck in Abstract Reasoning Benchmarks
Snippet: Reasoning benchmarks such as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) and ARC-AGI are widely used to assess progress in artificial intelligence and are often interpreted as probes of core, so-called ``fluid''reasoning abilities. Despite their apparent simplicity for humans, these tasks remain challenging for frontier vision-language models (VLMs), a gap commonly attributed to deficiencies in machine reasoning. We challenge this interpretation and hypothesize that the gap arises primarily from limitations in visual perception rather than from shortcomings in inductive reasoning. To verify this hypothesis, we introduce a two-stage experimental pipeline that explicitly separates perception and reasoning. In the perception stage, each image is independently converted into a natural-language description, while in the reasoning stage a model induces and applies rules using these descriptions. This design prevents leakage of cross-image inductive signals and isolates reasoning from perception bottlenecks. Across three ARC-style datasets, Mini-ARC, ACRE, and Bongard-LOGO, we show that the perception capability is the dominant factor underlying the observed performance gap by comparing the two-stage pipeline with against standard end-to-end one-stage evaluation. Manual inspection of reasoning traces in the VLM outputs further reveals that approximately 80 percent of model failures stem from perception errors. Together, these results demonstrate that ARC-style benchmarks conflate perceptual and reasoning challenges and that observed performance gaps may overstate deficiencies in machine reasoning. Our findings underscore the need for evaluation protocols that disentangle perception from reasoning when assessing progress in machine intelligence.
</snippet>

Title: EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning
Snippet: A long-standing goal of artificial intelligence research is to develop systems that can reason and answer questions about visual information. Numerous benchmarks assess the visual reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs). Previous work has created Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmarks where the model is asked (open-ended) questions about understanding a real world scene generated synthetically or created from real-world data [2] [7]. Other benchmarks include datasets of geometry problems with image components [11] [3]. However, these benchmarks focus on extracting information rather than true visual understanding and reasoning. In this paper, we introduce EasyARC: a true visual reasoning benchmark inspired from the abstract reasoning challenge ARC [5]. We believe EasyARC addresses a crucial gap in multimodal AI: the ability to perform true visual reasoning beyond simple information extraction. 

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the ARC challenge and consequently EasyARC with our motivation behind creating the dataset. In Section 3, we evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on EasyARC, demonstrating that current models fail on this very simple benchmark. Furthermore, we explore failure modes of these models in an attempt to understand missing components for this task and plot future research directions.
